turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit down, you're very welcome. What brought you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah I'm grand, I nearly talked myself out of coming. It's probably a waste of your time.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not a waste at all. Tell me what's been happening, however you want to put it.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's just a small bit of a pain, up here on the right under the ribs. Comes on after the fry or cheese, anything greasy.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right side, under the ribs, after the greasy food. What does it feel like when it's there?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): A deep ache, more than a sharp thing. I'm grand between times, so I don't know why I'm fussing.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And once it starts, how long before it lets go?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I was going to say all evening. Umm, well actually no, two or three hours and then it eases. It's been about three months, an antacid takes the edge off, and I was sick with it the once. I'm making it sound worse than it is.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Three months is worth a look, even if you're playing it down. Anything else you notice when the pain is on you?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. I just wait it out. Put the kettle on, that sort of thing.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): You said you were sick the once. Was that vomiting, and did it happen again?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Vomited, yeah, err, just the once, a couple of weeks back after a roast. Nothing since. Hardly worth mentioning.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you been taking anything for it?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): That gaviscn from the chemist. I thought it was two spoons, well actually it's one spoon, the 10 ml, when the pain starts. My sister keeps pushing her omeprozole on me but that's hers, I don't take it.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. So gaviscon, 10 ml, when the pain starts, and not your sister's tablet. Does it do much?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Takes the edge off, that's all. I'm not looking for a miracle.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anyone in the family had trouble like this?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother had her gallbladder out, years ago. She was far worse than me. That's the only one.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Your mother had the gallbladder removed. Anyone else?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): My husband John is on metformin for his diabetes, two tablets a day, but that's his sugar, not mine. I don't take a thing of his.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave his metformin well alone. Now, any fever with these pains, or do you feel shivery?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fever. I'm not shivery either.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): And chest wise, any cough, or getting short of breath?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Chest is fine. I can walk the length of the town.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has your weight changed at all?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah no. Well, the jeans feel a small bit loose, or maybe they just stretched, umm I haven't been on the scales. No, I'm the same weight I've always been.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): So no weight loss, then?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): The thing that actually annoyed me today was the bus. Forty minutes from Salthill in the rain, and the radio hurling cutting out.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Was the rain that bad on the coast road?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Sheets of it. And I missed the last ten minutes of the match stuck at the lights. Galway were doing tidy enough before that.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ah that's frustrating. Who were they playing?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't even catch the name properly, the reception was desperate. My neighbour's lad is on the under sixteens, he was practising in the garden in all that wet.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Practising in that? Fair play to him.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): His nan knitted him a scarf in the wrong colours entirely. We were in stitches over it. Purple and orange, if you can imagine.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Purple and orange, lord. Did he wear it anyway?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): He did, to please her. He's a good kid. Anyway, that's me rambling, sorry.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't be sorry, it's nice to hear. Let me come back to your tummy, if I may. Lie back and I'll have a feel.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on. It's only a bit sore, I'm not going to leap off the bed.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): The tummy is soft. Tender under the right ribs, and sore when you breathe in there. No guarding, and nothing rigid.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. That's the spot. Still only mild, though.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): I think this is most likely biliary colic, the gallbladder acting up after fatty food. I wouldn't call it certain until we see the tests.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Gallbladder. Sure I'm nothing like my mother was. She couldn't keep a cup of tea down.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): You can be milder and it still be the same sort of thing. I'd like a full blood count, liver blood tests, and an ultrasound of the tummy.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): An ultrasound for this? It feels like a lot of fuss.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll book the bloods and the ultrasound. Bloods can be done downstairs today, and the scan as soon as there's a slot. Not a fuss, just a proper look.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Of. Grand, so. If you say so.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ease off the fry and the cheese in the meantime. Stick with the gaviscon, 10 ml, when it niggles.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): I can leave the rashers. I'll miss them, but I can.

[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the pain turns severe, or you can't keep fluids down with vomiting, or you get a fever, or the whites of the eyes go yellow, go to the emergency department and don't wait for me.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Yellow eyes. I hear you. I doubt it'll come to that.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in two weeks and we'll go through the results together.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. I'll be grand, I'm sure of it. I'll bring a brolly next time.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do. Mind yourself on the way out, it's still pouring.

spec.situation: Woman with right-upper stomach pain after fatty meals, lasting hours, once with vomiting; takes antacid; mother had gallbladder surgery; blood tests and ultrasound planned.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

bad.reason: Husband's diabetes is not family history of the patient.

omissions.text: Examination finding of inspiratory arrest/pain on breathing in over the right upper quadrant (positive Murphy's sign): 'sore when you breathe in there.'
Recorded family history is wrong: husband John being on metformin for diabetes is not the patient's family history and should not be recorded as such.
Medication history detail omitted: patient specifically denies taking her sister's omeprazole and denies taking her husband's metformin.
Investigation logistics/planning detail omitted: blood tests can be done downstairs today, and ultrasound to be arranged as soon as a slot is available.
